text: Take 5g a day as a baseline, to keep your enterocytes fed. Take it away from meals, so it doesn't have to compete with the amino acids in your food to get absorbed. If you train hard or long, like CrossFit or intense cardio, your gut lining takes damage. While you train, your body sends blood away from your gut to your working muscles, so your enterocytes get less oxygen and fuel. Glutamine taken two hours before training helps with that. In a study of men running for an hour in the heat, their gut lining leaked less, even at the lowest dose tested, about 15g for a 70kg man. If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure to toxins or pathogens, or your whole system is under a lot of stress, raise it to 10-30g a day, adding 1g a day in case you're sensitive to it. Up to 14g a day is known to be safe for the long run, but the studies of higher doses were too short to say, so come back down once it's over. If you have an active inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), like Crohn's or colitis, don't count on it. In the two small trials in active Crohn's, it didn't help.
section: Some Causes of poor gut health
reader: Someone with a leaky gut deciding whether and how to take glutamine (how much, when, and at what risk, cancer included), and where butyrate fits.

sentences.s: Take 5g a day as a baseline, to keep your enterocytes fed.
sentences.payoff: The reader knows the everyday dose and what it's for, whether or not they train (his card 4, approved).
sentences.follows: It gives the dose right after the paragraph on how glutamine feeds the enterocytes.

sentences.s: Take it away from meals, so it doesn't have to compete with the amino acids in your food to get absorbed.
sentences.payoff: The reader knows when to take it, and why: the amino acids in food compete with it (his F9-5 answer).
sentences.follows: How to take the dose follows the dose.

sentences.s: If you train hard or long, like CrossFit or intense cardio, your gut lining takes damage.
sentences.payoff: A reader who trains hard learns their training damages the gut lining, so the 5g isn't the whole story for them.
sentences.follows: Training comes next as the case that needs more than the baseline.

sentences.s: While you train, your body sends blood away from your gut to your working muscles, so your enterocytes get less oxygen and fuel.
sentences.payoff: The reader understands how exercise damages the gut, though exercise is good for them elsewhere in the post: blood leaves the gut for the muscles.
sentences.follows: It answers how the training in the sentence before does the damage.

sentences.s: Glutamine taken two hours before training helps with that.
sentences.payoff: A reader who trains learns what to do about it: take it two hours before.
sentences.follows: The fix follows the damage just explained.

sentences.s: In a study of men running for an hour in the heat, their gut lining leaked less, even at the lowest dose tested, about 15g for a 70kg man.
sentences.payoff: The reader knows the dose and timing that helped, about 15g, not 5g, and the evidence behind it (Pugh 2017).
sentences.follows: The study supports the advice in the sentence before, right after it.

sentences.s: If your immune system is dealing with an acute exposure to toxins or pathogens, or your whole system is under a lot of stress, raise it to 10-30g a day, adding 1g a day in case you're sensitive to it.
sentences.payoff: The reader knows the other cases that call for more, what an exposure is (toxins or pathogens), and how to raise it: a gram a day, in case of sensitivity (his F9-5 answers).
sentences.follows: After training, the other cases that need more than the baseline, as in his sentence.

sentences.s: Up to 14g a day is known to be safe for the long run, but the studies of higher doses were too short to say, so come back down once it's over.
sentences.payoff: The reader knows how high is safe for how long, so they come back down after the exposure or stress (Shao and Hathcock 2008).
sentences.follows: The safety limit follows the higher dose it applies to.

sentences.s: If you have an active inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), like Crohn's or colitis, don't count on it.
sentences.payoff: A reader with active IBD won't count on glutamine for it; IBD gets its full name here, at its first mention.
sentences.follows: After the cases where more helps, the case where the evidence says it doesn't.

sentences.s: In the two small trials in active Crohn's, it didn't help.
sentences.payoff: The reader knows why: the trials found no benefit (Cochrane 2016).
sentences.follows: The evidence follows the advice it supports.

checked.point: glutamine before a run cut the gut's leak, even at the lowest dose
checked.found: Pugh 2017: 0.25, 0.5 and 0.9 g per kg of fat-free mass two hours before a 60-minute run at 30 C all lowered the permeability marker; 0.9 g/kg is 54g for a 70kg man at 15% fat, so 0.25 is about 15g (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5694515/)
checked.still_needed: yes: it gives the training reader a dose that was tested

checked.point: up to 14g a day is safe long term
checked.found: Shao and Hathcock 2008: observed safe level 14 g/day; higher intakes tested without harm but not enough data for long-term safety (https://www.nutraingredients.com/Article/2008/04/18/crn-authors-risk-assessment-for-key-amino-acids/)

checked.point: take amino acids away from meals
checked.found: amino acids share transporters and can compete; there is too little human research to know at what dose, so labels say to take them without food (https://www.consumerlab.com/answers/must-i-take-amino-acid-supplements-on-an-empty-stomach/how_to_take_amino_acid)
checked.still_needed: yes: his answer, with its reason

checked.found: Cochrane 2016: two small trials found no benefit; insufficient evidence (https://www.cochrane.org/CD007348)
checked.still_needed: yes: the original raised the dose for active IBD
